title: From Conjecture to Proof: Brewer's CAP Talk and the Gilbert-Lynch Paper (2000-2002)
explainer: Eric Brewer presented the CAP tradeoff (consistency, availability, partition tolerance) as an informal conjecture in a 2000 PODC keynote; it only became a citable, provable theorem when Seth Gilbert and Nancy Lynch formalized the definitions and proved it in a 2002 paper. That gap between an influential talk and a rigorous, reproducible written proof is itself a useful case study for a lesson on reading and reproducing systems papers - including why the formal versions of 'consistency' and 'availability' in the proof are narrower than the everyday systems-engineering meanings people often assume.

resources.title: Brewer's Conjecture and the Feasibility of Consistent, Available, Partition-Tolerant Web Services

title: The End-to-End Argument: A Design Paper Every Systems Course Still Assigns (1984)
explainer: Saltzer, Reed, and Clark's 1984 paper argued that functions like reliability or security should usually live at the endpoints of a system rather than be duplicated in every intermediate layer, since only the endpoints can implement them completely and correctly. Decades later it remains one of the most reproduced and re-argued papers in systems design, making it a good concrete example of how a short, carefully reasoned systems paper gets read, re-derived, and debated long after publication.
